Pooled over dev_a it is +0.78 (22 wrong→right, 18 right→wrong over 512), just below the +0.8 futility threshold I set before this pass, so the C(−1.0) line stops. Even with perfect follow-up, the original +1.9 DEV bar would require about +3.0 on each of dev_b1 and dev_b2, far above anything any C variant has produced there.

The two doses do behave as the flip proxy predicted. C(−1.0) frees fewer loops (cut-offs 21% and 18%, against 14% and 15% for C(−1.5)) and causes fewer losses on finished answers. On dev_a it scores about 2 points above C(−1.5), but that is unpaired between doses, measured on the set used to build the direction, and within noise. I'm restoring the frozen submission C(−1.5) from /work/best_final and verifying it byte for byte.

The submission C(−1.5) is restored and verified. Six passes remain, which is not enough to build and fully validate a new edit, so any further work should explain the edit's one known weakness. That weakness is the net loss on problems the original finished: 70 wrong→right against 97 right→wrong. This analysis uses no pass. I'll take the right→wrong cases among originally finished problems across all C(−1.5) generation passes (13, 28, 29–33, 39, 40). Each lost answer is sorted three ways: the edit made it loop (now cut), it ended with a different wrong number, or it changed solution style. Style is judged by the first token, "Let" (plain) against "Here" (markdown), which I earlier found tied to accuracy. If many losses are newly cut answers, C also creates loops in some problems. If most are style changes, the collateral damage acts through the style-switch effect seen earlier. Either finding is useful in the report, even without a pass left to act on it.

Among the originally finished problems that C(−1.5) turned wrong (97), 16% now loop to the token limit. The rest finish with a different wrong number, in answers that run on average 1.42 times longer, against 1.05 for the gains. No loss comes from a change of solution style: the first token never changes, and in about 60% of cases the first 120 characters are identical. Overall, 105 of 1,665 originally finished answers (6.3%) become cut under C. So the edit does not only free loops: it moves the loop boundary, freeing about 60% of the original's loops while causing new ones, or longer, drifting reasoning, in a small share of answers that had been fine. That explains the modest net gain and its variability between sets.

Six passes cannot both build and validate a correction for those new loops on DEV and HOLDOUT, so I won't start a new edit. I'll record this finding and the final plan in the notes.
